idiom_name: newtype struct Orders(Vec<Order>) with validating methods; AsRef<[Order]>/IntoIterator for exposure
implementation_notes: The idiomatic realization is the newtype: `pub struct Orders(Vec<Order>)` keeps the field private, so the only way to build or change the collection is through your methods, and those methods return Result when an invariant is violated. Reads are exposed as borrowed slices - as_slice()/AsRef<[Order]>, plus IntoIterator<Item = &Order> for for-loops - so callers can iterate, sort a copy or pass the data to anything that wants &[T] without ever owning the Vec. Do not implement Deref<Target = Vec<Order>> or to [Order] for an invariant-carrying collection: the Rust API guidelines reserve Deref for smart pointers, and deref coercion would hand callers push, sort, retain and splice - exactly the leak the pattern exists to close. Derive Clone/Debug/Default as appropriate and add TryFrom<Vec<Order>> as the validating constructor.
pitfalls: Deref to Vec/slice silently re-exposes push/sort/splice and lets callers pass the wrapper where the bare collection is expected; delegate explicitly (Rust API guidelines C-DEREF).
The tuple field is private only while it is not marked pub: `pub struct Orders(pub Vec<Order>)` gives the invariants away.
clone on the wrapper copies the elements; cloning per access turns the collection into an allocation hot spot - expose &[Order] instead.
Returning &Vec<Order> rather than &[Order] freezes the internal representation and forces callers to accept the container choice.
